evidence.text: One stroke on top of another; compare 下 (below)
Originally a small line or dot above a longer line, indicating "up". The vertical line was added to distinguish the character from 二 (two).

Ideogram (指事): a line above another (contrast 下 (xià)) — up. Originally written as 𠄞, but changed to this form to prevent confusion with 二 (èr).
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *tVŋ (“top”). Cognate with Tibetan སྟེང (steng), Tibetan ཡང་རྩེ (yang rtse, “summit; pinnacle”) (Bodman, 1980), Mizo zo (“to be high”), zah (“to respect; to revere”) (STEDT).
Shijing rimes indicate occasional level tone for pronunciation 2 (Schuessler, 2007).
Pronunciation 1 is the exopassive of pronunciation 2 with suffix *-s, literally meaning "what has been raised" (Schuessler, 2007). The rising tone in Middle Chinese words with voiced stop initials regularly evolves into departing tone in Mandarin. Pronunciation 3 results from 叶韻 (xiéyùn), i.e. its pronunciation has been artificially changed to preserve rhymes in classical poetry.

evidence.field: 漢字甲骨部件分析 / 上 / 字形與用例
evidence.text: The database describes the oracle-bone graph as a short stroke above a baseline, which could be curved in early forms and was often straightened in later forms because straight horizontal lines were easier to carve. It reports that early oracle-bone and bronze forms were similar to 二, with a vertical stroke added in late Spring-and-Autumn bronze forms to distinguish 上 from 下 and 二. It gives the original meaning as 'above/upper side.' Its examples include oracle-bone 上帝 (Heji 16703), 上甲 (Heji 6384), and a paired 上/下 passage (Heji 6204); Zhou bronze examples include 上 meaning 'above,' as in 㝬鐘, and 'on/at the side of,' as in 啟尊. These are source-reported readings and examples, not direct inspection of the inscribed artifacts here.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 香港教育局 字源考釋
evidence.field: 字形流變 / 字形解說
evidence.text: This character-specific account presents oracle-bone 上 as two horizontal strokes, the longer lower stroke representing a horizon and the shorter upper stroke marking 'above.' It says later bronze and small-seal forms changed the upper stroke to a vertical stroke to avoid confusion with 二, and the modern standard graph adds a dot. This differs in detail from the CUHK account's curved-baseline description, though both identify a positional marker above a reference line and later graphic differentiation.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 — 上

evidence.field: 上 / semantic uses by inscriptional period
evidence.text: The dictionary separately reports Shang oracle-bone uses in 上帝, 上甲, and 上/下 contrasts; Zhou bronze uses include spatial 'above,' 'at/on the side of,' and 上帝, and it cites a Spring-and-Autumn-period tally where 以上 means 'more than.' It also notes a Chu-script form with 辵 added as a semantic element for movement upward. These reports show that spatial and lexical uses are attested in inscriptional contexts, but the listed examples do not establish a precise chronology for every later sense such as 'superior,' 'ruler,' or the verb 'ascend.'

Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

items.period: Shuowen seal-script style; modern vector rendering, not a dated artifact
items.caption: This Shuowen seal-script-style rendering has an upper stroke that bends right and descends into a central upright, above a long horizontal baseline. It illustrates a received seal-style form without establishing a dated transition from an earlier graph.
items.alt: A black glyph with a long horizontal baseline, a central upright, and an upper stroke that curves right and down into the upright.
items.selection_reason: The rendering provides a useful example of 上 in Shuowen seal-script style. Its visible form is distinct from the simple upper mark and reference line described for early forms, but it does not establish a historical sequence between them.
items.rights: CC0 1.0 / public domain; attribution is not required but appreciated.

limitations.text: This is a modern seal-script-style rendering, not a dated artifact image. The early reference line is described as curved in some accounts and horizontal in others; this image does not resolve that variation or date a transition.
